purpose: Code is read and changed by a maintainer, a person or an AI, who takes it over to change what a product does. The code is built to a specification: the behaviors it is asked to give, such as requirements or a design. The maintainer sets the code up from what it declares and sees from its tests that it gives each behavior the specification asks. They find where a change belongs and call what they did not write without reading every body. After a change, the tests tell them whether every behavior still holds. Whoever runs the code gets those behaviors, and where the code stops on something wrong from outside, learns from what it says how to put it right.

format.skeleton:
<The manifest: the runtime and each library the code needs, each with the versions it runs on, and the command that runs the tests>

<For each module, a file>

<Its opening comment: what this module alone decides, in a sentence or two>

<For each name other modules use: its signature, with the types it takes and gives, and a comment saying what it gives, what it expects of what it takes, and each way it refuses>

<The body>

<For each module, a test file beside it>

<For each case of the specification: a test named for the behavior it holds, its body in three parts: Given <the situation>, When <what is done>, Then <what must be so>>

parts.what: The file the language's tools read for what the code needs: the runtime and each library with the versions it runs on, and the command that runs the tests.
parts.why: The maintainer sets the code up and runs its tests from this file alone.

parts.what: The comment at the top of each module: what this module alone decides.
parts.why: The maintainer finds the module a change belongs in by reading openings, not bodies.

parts.what: Each name a module offers to others: its signature with its types, and the comment above or below it on what it gives, what it expects and each way it refuses.
parts.why: The maintainer calls code they did not write from its interface alone.

parts.what: The code under each interface that gives the behavior.
parts.why: It gives the behaviors the specification asks; the maintainer changes it.

parts.what: A test file beside each module, one test for each case of the specification, named for the behavior it holds, its body as Given, When and Then.
parts.why: The maintainer sees which behavior each test holds and, after a change, whether each still holds.

checklist.what: When the maintainer sets the code up on a fresh machine with only what the manifest names, and runs the tests again and in any order, do they pass every time?
checklist.why: If yes, the maintainer starts work from the manifest alone, and a failing test means the code broke, nothing else. The manifest names every runtime and library with its versions, and each test sets up and clears what it needs, so its result rests on the code alone. If no, the code works only where its writer had something installed, and fails on the next machine for a reason no one was told; a test that passes on one run and fails on the next teaches the maintainer to ignore failures, real ones included.
grounds: The Twelve-Factor App, "II. Dependencies": "A twelve-factor app never relies on implicit existence of system-wide packages." and "It declares all dependencies, completely and exactly, via a dependency declaration manifest."

Winters, Manshreck and Wright, Software Engineering at Google, ch. 11 "Testing Overview": "It doesn't take needing to investigate many flakes before a team loses trust in the test suite." and "a test should contain all of the information necessary to set up, execute, and tear down its environment."

examples.fails: The manifest names fastapi with no version, and the booking tests read the machine's clock and a database the writer had running. (On a fresh machine a newer fastapi breaks the API, and a hold test fails each day after 23:45.)
examples.passes: The manifest names Python 3.12, fastapi 0.115 and the test command; each booking test starts its own database and sets the clock it needs.

checklist.what: When the maintainer has one behavior to change, can they tell from the modules' opening comments alone which module to open?
checklist.why: If yes, the maintainer goes to the one module that decides the thing they change, without reading every body. Each module hides one decision from the others, and its opening says which. If no, the maintainer reads module after module to find the place, or changes the first likely one, and the behavior is decided in two places from then on.
grounds: Google Python Style Guide, Modules: "Files should start with a docstring describing the contents and usage of the module."

Parnas, "On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules" (1972): "one begins with a list of difficult design decisions or design decisions which are likely to change. Each module is then designed to hide such a decision from the others."

examples.fails: """Room utilities.""" (Asked to let a room with one seat short still fit when an attendee is remote, the maintainer opens rooms.py, matcher.py and utils.py.)
examples.passes: """Decides whether a room fits a meeting: a seat for each attendee in the room and every piece of equipment the meeting needs. No other module judges a fit."""

checklist.what: When the maintainer calls a function or a class another module offers, can they write a call that works from its signature and comment alone, without reading its body?
checklist.why: If yes, the maintainer uses code they did not write at once, and each module can change inside while its callers stay. The interface says what it takes, what it gives, what it expects and each way it refuses. If no, the maintainer reads the body to learn what to pass and what comes back, and comes to rely on how it works inside; a case the interface leaves unsaid, such as what comes back when nothing is found, is handled one way by one caller and another way by the next.
grounds: Google Python Style Guide, Functions and Methods: "A docstring should give enough information to write a call to the function without reading the function's code." and, of Raises: "List all exceptions that are relevant to the interface followed by a description."

examples.passes:
def rooms_that_fit(meeting: Meeting, rooms: list[Room]) -> list[Room]:
    """The rooms with a seat for each attendee and all the meeting's equipment, in the order given; empty when none fits. Raises ValueError when the meeting has no attendees."""

checklist.what: When something the code takes from outside is wrong, such as a malformed input or a missing file, can whoever ran the code put it right from what the code tells them alone?
checklist.why: If yes, they fix the cause and run again, and nothing was left half done. The code checks what comes from outside where it comes in, before acting on it, and its message says what was wrong, where, and what is accepted; inside, each part trusts what it is given. If no, a bad value travels on and fails far from its cause with a message about the place it failed, or passes silently and gives a wrong result, and whoever ran it cannot tell what to change or what was already done.
grounds: Nielsen Norman Group, "10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design", #9: "Error messages should be expressed in plain language (no error codes), precisely indicate the problem, and constructively suggest a solution."
OWASP, "Input Validation Cheat Sheet": "validate the resulting values before business processing or storage".
Peters, "PEP 20 - The Zen of Python": "Errors should never pass silently."

examples.fails: A booking with "attendees": "six" is held, then fails in the matcher with "TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'". (The worker cannot tell what to change, and the room stays held.)
examples.passes: The Booking API holds nothing and refuses the request at once with: attendees must be a whole number from 1 to 200; got "six".

checklist.what: When the maintainer asks of any case the specification names, its edges and refusals included, "Which test holds this?", can they point to one?
checklist.why: If yes, every behavior asked has a test that checks what the specification says of it, and the test's name and its Given, When and Then tell which case it holds, so a failure names the behavior broken. The cases come from the specification, not from the code, as a test drawn from the code holds what the code does, not what it must. If no, a case with no test breaks unseen on the next change, and a test whose name does not say its case leaves the maintainer to read it to learn what broke.
grounds: Winters, Manshreck and Wright, Software Engineering at Google, ch. 12 "Unit Testing": "A behavior is any guarantee that a system makes about how it will respond to a series of inputs" and "A test's name should summarize the behavior it is testing."
Fowler, "GivenWhenThen" (martinfowler.com): "The given part describes the state of the world before you begin the behavior you're specifying in this scenario."

examples.fails: test_match() books a six-person meeting into a ten-seat room. (The specification says a room with exactly as many seats fits and a meeting needing a screen gets no room without one; neither has a test.)
examples.passes: test_room_with_exactly_enough_seats_fits, test_room_one_seat_short_does_not_fit, test_room_without_needed_screen_does_not_fit and test_meeting_with_no_attendees_is_refused, each as Given, When and Then.

checklist.what: When the maintainer breaks a behavior a test holds, such as by turning a comparison around, does that test fail?
checklist.why: If yes, a passing run tells the maintainer that each behavior the tests hold still holds, and they change the code on that trust. Each test checks the result the specification asks, not only that the code ran. If no, a test that passes whatever the code does gives the trust without the check, and a broken behavior reaches the product's users with every test green.
grounds: Google, "What to look for in a code review" (google/eng-practices), Tests: "Will the tests actually fail when the code is broken?"
Stryker Mutator, documentation: "Mutation testing introduces changes to your code, then runs your unit tests against the changed code. It is expected that your unit tests will now fail."

examples.fails: The test runs rooms_that_fit and checks only that it returns a list. (Changing seats >= attendees to seats > attendees still passes.)
examples.passes: The test checks that a ten-seat room is offered for ten attendees and not for eleven, so turning >= into > fails it.

checklist.what: When the maintainer asks of any behavior the code has, such as an option, a mode or a case it handles, "Which case of the specification needs this?", can they answer?
checklist.why: If yes, every behavior the maintainer keeps, tests and changes around serves a case someone asked for, and a behavior is removed once its case is gone. If no, a behavior no case needs is kept, tested and worked around by every maintainer after, and no one dares remove it, as no one can tell who relies on it.
grounds: Google, "What to look for in a code review" (google/eng-practices), Complexity: "A particular type of complexity is over-engineering, where developers have made the code more generic than it needs to be, or added functionality that isn't presently needed by the system."

Fowler, "Yagni" (martinfowler.com, 2015): "The code for the presumptive feature adds some complexity to the software, this complexity makes it harder to modify and debug that software, thus increasing the cost of other features."

examples.fails: rooms_that_fit takes strategy="best" | "first" | "random" and a cache_ttl, where the specification asks for the rooms that fit, in one order.
examples.passes: rooms_that_fit takes the meeting and the rooms, and gives the rooms that fit in the order given.
